name: Concussion and Other Traumatic Brain Injuries

clinicalPearls: TBI is defined as an externally caused alteration in brain function or other evidence of brain pathology, marked by any of the following: loss/decrease in consciousness, retrograde or posttraumatic amnesia, neurologic deficits, or altered mental state at the moment of injury (p.3571).

Incidence shows a bimodal age distribution: motor vehicle crashes predominate in younger persons (more often men), while falls are the leading cause in older adults (more often women); roughly 70-90% (most estimates ~85%) of treated TBIs are mild (p.3570, p.3572).

Severity is graded with the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS): mild 13-15, moderate 9-12, severe 3-8; the individual eye/verbal/motor components (e.g., E3V4M6) are more informative than the summed total, which should only describe groups (p.3571).

In moderate-to-severe TBI, GCS plus the duration of loss of consciousness (LOC) and posttraumatic amnesia (PTA) predict outcome well; in mild TBI, LOC and PTA are far less predictive of recovery time and outcome, and postinjury symptom burden is the most robust predictor (p.3571, p.3574).

Epidural hematoma classically follows tearing of the middle meningeal artery beneath a temporal-bone fracture, evolves rapidly, and may be preceded by a lucid interval; rapid surgical evacuation usually yields a favorable outcome (p.3572).

Acute subdural hematoma is usually venous in origin, can occur without major trauma (especially in the elderly or anticoagulated, or from acceleration/whiplash forces), and carries significant morbidity and mortality when surgery is required - in contrast to the generally better-treated epidural hematoma (p.3572).

Contusions follow coup (under the impact) and contrecoup (antipolar) mechanisms; blunt deceleration typically bruises the orbitofrontal and anterior/basal temporal lobes, and old contusion sites become gliotic scars that are highly epileptogenic (p.3573).

Traumatic axonal injury (TAI) from shearing forces is among the most common TBI lesions; four or more foci constitute diffuse axonal injury (DAI), which when widespread is proposed to underlie prolonged coma and the vegetative state (p.3573).

Anosmia and apparent loss of taste occur in ~10% of serious head injuries (especially falls onto the back of the head) from shearing of olfactory filaments at the cribriform plate; persistent bilateral anosmia for several months carries a poor prognosis (p.3573-3574).

Second-impact syndrome is a rare, often fatal diffuse cerebral swelling that follows a second minor head injury before the first has resolved - a key reason no athlete should return to play until fully asymptomatic and cleared (p.3575).

Blood biomarkers GFAP (astroglial injury) and UCHL1 (neuronal injury) are now usable at point of care; GFAP in particular discriminates intracranial abnormalities and helps stratify CT+, CT-/MRI+, and CT-/MRI- patients, with both diagnostic and prognostic value (p.3574).

Chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) - tau deposition in superficial cortical layers, perivascular regions, and the depths of sulci - is linked to repetitive head impacts but remains a postmortem diagnosis; proposed clinical criteria lack specificity and in vivo imaging/biomarker findings have been inconsistent (p.3576-3577).
harrison.pathophysiology: TBI results from external mechanical force - the head being struck or striking an object, acceleration/deceleration of the brain, penetration, or blast/explosion - producing primary structural lesions and secondary injury. A skull fracture marks the site and severity of impact and, when the arachnoid is torn, opens a pathway for CSF leak and bacterial entry (meningitis risk); basilar fractures may cause CSF leak, pneumocephalus, and delayed cavernous-carotid fistula. Extra-axial hematomas arise from torn meningeal arteries (epidural) or bridging veins (subdural) and exert mass effect that raises intracranial pressure. Cortical surface bruising (contusion) occurs at coup and contrecoup sites with petechial hemorrhage, edema, and tissue destruction. Shearing of axons (traumatic/diffuse axonal injury) at impact, with associated microhemorrhages, disrupts white-matter connectivity. Traumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage from rupture of small cortical vessels is common and, when diffuse after severe TBI, increases mortality. In concussion/mild TBI, conventional CT is often normal while higher-resolution 3T MRI may reveal contusion or microhemorrhage; advanced imaging shows reduced cerebral blood flow, altered functional connectivity, and white-matter microstructural change that broadly track injury severity and recovery, though subtle changes may persist after clinical recovery (a neurobiologic recovery 'tail').
additionalDifferentials: Postconcussion symptom overlap with preinjury mood or anxiety disorders (e.g., depression, PTSD)
Transient ischemic attack (chronic subdural hematoma may mimic with brief hemiparesis or aphasia)
Intracranial neoplasm or abscess (evolving contusion with surrounding enhancement and edema can be mistaken for these)
Carotid or vertebral artery dissection presenting as focal deficit after trauma
Drug or alcohol intoxication confounding the neurologic exam
Cervical spine injury (may be clinically inapparent)
nonInfectiousMimics: Chronic subdural hematoma mimicking TIA, dementia, or personality change in the elderly
Contusion with delayed contrast enhancement mimicking tumor or abscess
Trochlear (fourth nerve) palsy after minor head injury mimicking primary ocular motility disorder
Persistent postconcussion symptoms attributable instead to preinjury psychiatric illness, migraine, or adjustment reaction
CTE clinical criteria overlapping with other neurodegenerative conditions (low specificity)
additionalInvestigations: Noncontrast CT - first-line for skull fracture, extra-axial hematoma, contusion, traumatic SAH, and large TAI lesions with blood

MRI (including gradient-echo/susceptibility-weighted and diffusion sequences) - more sensitive than CT for microhemorrhage and axonal injury; detects intracranial abnormalities in ~27% of CT-negative mild TBI patients and has prognostic value
Advanced/multimodal MRI (functional MRI, cerebral blood flow, diffusion) - increasing sensitivity for subtle injury
Blood-based biomarkers GFAP and UCHL1 - point-of-care detection and prognostication across the TBI spectrum
GCS scoring before sedation/paralysis or intubation
Validated symptom inventories (e.g., Rivermead Post-Concussion Symptom Questionnaire) to quantify and track recovery
Intracranial pressure monitoring (ventricular catheter or fiberoptic device) in severe TBI to guide therapy (note: has not been shown to improve outcome)
Cervical spine imaging given risk of concurrent occult injury
redFlags: Lucid interval followed by neurologic deterioration (suggests epidural or, less often, subdural hematoma)
Stupor or coma, hemiparesis, and unilateral pupillary enlargement (larger hematoma with mass effect)
Coma from the moment of injury - requires immediate resuscitation and neurologic attention

Persistent confusion, repeated vomiting (two or more episodes), palpable skull fracture, seizure, or >30 min of retrograde/persistent anterograde amnesia - sensitive indicators of intracranial hemorrhage warranting CT
Age >65 years, underlying coagulopathy or anticoagulant use, or concurrent serious bodily injury - lower the threshold for imaging
CSF leak (orthostatic headache, rhinorrhea/otorrhea), hemotympanum, Battle sign, or raccoon eyes - signs of basilar skull fracture
Large contusion or hemorrhage after only minor trauma - raises concern for coagulopathy or anticoagulation
Bilateral anosmia persisting for months - poor prognostic sign
harrison.prognosis: The typical concussion syndrome has a good prognosis with little risk of subsequent deterioration. After sport-related concussion, recovery is generally favorable: in a large collegiate cohort, median symptom resolution was about 6.4 days and median return to sport 12.8 days, with ~92% symptom resolution and ~85% clearance to return by one month; most athletes across ages fully recover over 1-4 weeks. A subset develop persistent postconcussion symptoms (PPCS) beyond ~3 months; preinjury mental health disorder, migraine, and prior concussion predispose to prolonged recovery. Recovery from severe TBI can take years, and long-term outcome prediction is limited and often incorrect; best practice recommends aggressive therapy for at least 72 h (absent brain death). TBI is now recognized as a chronic, dynamic condition, with meaningful improvement or decline observed 2-7 years post-injury regardless of initial severity. TBI (mild to severe) is associated with a 63-96% increased risk of all-cause dementia, with risk greatest after severe injury; TBI with LOC >1 h has been linked to subsequent Parkinson's disease and Lewy body accumulation.
pitfalls: Grading severity solely on acute injury characteristics can mislead - some severe TBI patients recover fully while some mild TBI patients have lifelong disability.
Relying on the summed GCS total rather than its components loses information; the score is confounded if recorded after sedation, paralysis, or intubation.
Assuming a normal CT excludes injury in mild TBI - MRI reveals intracranial abnormalities in about 27% of CT-negative patients and 3T MRI can show contusion/microhemorrhage.
Prescribing prolonged rest after concussion - inactivity beyond ~5 days can be detrimental and prolong recovery; supervised subthreshold exercise shortens symptom duration.
Overusing dependence-producing drugs for postconcussion symptoms.
Missing chronic subdural hematoma in the elderly, where trauma may be trivial or forgotten and the clot can become isodense and inapparent on CT between 2-6 weeks.
Overlooking concurrent occult cervical spine injury or drug/alcohol intoxication in injuries of intermediate severity.
Diagnosing CTE in vivo - it remains a postmortem diagnosis and proposed clinical criteria lack specificity.
Therapeutic nihilism in severe TBI, reinforced by the common but premature 6-month outcome endpoint - recovery may continue for years.
harrison.severityClassification: Glasgow Coma Scale-based grading: mild/concussion GCS 13-15, moderate GCS 9-12, severe GCS 3-8 (scores range 3-15). Mild TBI with CT and/or MRI abnormality is termed 'complicated mTBI' and carries a higher risk of unfavorable outcome. Loss of consciousness and posttraumatic amnesia duration further characterize severity. CTE neuropathology has been proposed to be staged as 'low' or 'high' severity (criteria not yet established).
management: Stabilise with attention to airway, breathing and circulation and cervical spine protection, scoring the Glasgow Coma Scale before sedation, and obtain a noncontrast CT to triage structural injury
Refer for urgent neurosurgical evacuation of extra-axial haematomas, such as an epidural or acute subdural collection causing mass effect

In severe injury, prevent secondary brain injury by maintaining oxygenation and cerebral perfusion, avoiding hypotension and hypoxia, and managing raised intracranial pressure with head elevation, sedation, osmotherapy using mannitol or hypertonic saline, and ventricular drainage
Consider early seizure prophylaxis with an antiepileptic after severe traumatic brain injury
Reverse anticoagulation promptly in patients with intracranial haemorrhage
Manage concussion with a brief period of relative physical and cognitive rest followed by a graded, symptom-limited return to activity and sport
Track recovery with validated symptom inventories and refer for neurorehabilitation where symptoms persist
